facts.statement: A corporation has an insurable interest in its directors, officers, employees, and others whose death or disability might cause it financial loss.
facts.quote: (a) in the life or physical or mental ability of any of its directors, officers, or employees, or the directors, officers, or employees of any of its subsidiaries or any other person whose death or physical or mental disability might cause financial loss to the corporation

items.stem: A corporation buys a life policy on its chief engineer, who designs its main products. Under New Jersey law, does the corporation have an insurable interest in the engineer's life?
options: Yes, but only if the engineer is also an officer
No, since only relatives have an insurable interest
No, since a corporation can insure only its owners
Yes, since the engineer's death could cause it financial loss
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-1.1 gives a corporation an insurable interest in its directors, officers and employees, and in anyone whose death or disability might cause it financial loss.
items.retired: Flagged as test-wise in two rounds: the financial-loss reason is identifiable by common sense among conditional options.

facts.statement: A corporation has an insurable interest in a shareholder's life to carry out an agreement to reacquire the shareholder's shares at death or disability.
facts.quote: pursuant to any contractual arrangement with any shareholder concerning the reacquisition of shares owned by him at the time of his death or disability

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, a corporation that has agreed to buy back a shareholder's stock at the shareholder's death has an insurable interest in that shareholder's life:
options: For the purpose of carrying out that agreement
For any amount, without regard to the agreement
Only while the shareholder is also an officer
Only after the shareholder's family consents
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-1.1 gives a corporation an insurable interest in a shareholder's life to carry out a contractual arrangement to reacquire the shareholder's shares at death or disability.
items.retired: Test-wise in two rounds: the statute's purpose wording makes the key stand out against conditional options. Business insurance needs a scenario-rich source.

facts.statement: Absent an exception, an employer's tax-free death proceeds on employer-owned life insurance are limited to the premiums and other amounts it paid.
facts.quote: shall not exceed an amount equal to the sum of the premiums and other amounts paid by the policyholder for the contract

items.stem: A company owned a policy on a staff accountant who was not a director or highly compensated when the policy was issued. Notice and consent were properly obtained. He left the company and died 5 years later. How are the death proceeds the company receives treated for income tax?
options: Taxable to the extent they exceed the premiums the company paid
Fully excluded, since notice and consent were obtained
Fully taxable, with no credit for premiums paid
Excluded, since key person coverage is tax-free
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(j) limits the exclusion to the premiums and other amounts paid unless an exception applies. Notice and consent alone are not enough; the insured must also fit an exception, such as being an employee within 12 months before death.

facts.statement: Employer-owned life insurance proceeds stay fully excludable, if notice and consent were met, when the insured was an employee at any time in the 12 months before death.
facts.quote: was an employee at any time during the 12-month period before the insured’s death

items.stem: A company with proper notice and consent owns a policy on a sales manager, who dies while still employed there. The death proceeds the company receives are:
options: Taxable above the premiums paid, since the company owns the policy
Taxable, since the company was the beneficiary
Excluded, but reduced by the cash value at death
Fully excluded from the company's gross income
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(j) keeps the full exclusion, when notice and consent were met, for an insured who was an employee at any time during the 12 months before death.

facts.statement: The employee's written notice and consent for employer-owned life insurance must be obtained before the contract is issued.
facts.quote: The notice and consent requirements of this paragraph are met if, before the issuance of the contract, the employee

items.stem: For employer-owned life insurance, when must the employee receive written notice and give written consent?
options: Before the policy is issued
Within 30 days after the policy is issued
Before the employer files a death claim
Within 12 months after employment ends
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(j) requires the employee's written notice and consent before the issuance of the contract.

facts.statement: The written notice must tell the employee the maximum face amount for which he or she could be insured.
facts.quote: the maximum face amount for which the employee could be insured at the time the contract was issued

items.stem: Under federal tax rules on employer-owned life insurance, the employer's written notice to the employee must state:
options: The premium the employer will pay each year
The employee's own share of the cash value
The rating class the insurer assigned
The maximum face amount for which the employee could be insured
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(j) requires written notice of the employer's intent to insure the employee and of the maximum face amount for which the employee could be insured.
